world: A paper street of four named sites at dusk. Rolling shutters slam down door after door while nobody is outside; then a cartoon figure tagged HACKER rattles the closed shutters.
why: The hook is about choosing to close, not being broken into. Shopkeepers pulling shutters before a storm says 'on purpose' in a second and builds the street we return to.

world: A desk of index cards, one per site that closed, each getting an OFFLINE rubber stamp; the last one lands the joke.
why: A list ending on a punchline: each stamp is a beat, and the held last stamp lands 'four-chan'.

world: A paper restaurant: the viewer's phone on the left, the PHP kitchen on the right. An order flies in, the kitchen steams, a fresh page comes back.
why: Before the hole means anything, the viewer must see what PHP does: a cook making your page fresh when you open it.

world: Words as food: the stat slams in over sun rays, gets circled, then a DAL-CHAWAL stamp thumps down like a steel plate.
why: 'Nearly 7 in 10' is dry; dal-chawal makes it feel ordinary and everywhere, which is why one hole matters.

data.sub: of sites whose server language is known

world: The same kitchen, now facing a STRANGER. The kitchen's back door swings open, a red slip flies in, the kitchen turns red and a terminal types what the stranger cooks.
why: A callback to the kitchen we just learned. 'Running code on a server' becomes a stranger at the stove with no login, which anyone can picture.

world: A railway split-flap board: the severity rating slams in, the board rolls from 2012 to 2026, then a birthday cake with 14 candles pops up.
why: Two numbers, two things: 9.2 lands as a caption, and the door's age becomes a board rolling through the years and a cake you can count.

world: A hand-drawn team chat window labelled re-enactment: the flaw gets posted, typing dots blink, a jumble of contradicting replies types out, and a NO AGREEMENT stamp lands.
why: 'Couldn't agree on a fix' is abstract. A group chat that argues and decides nothing is the joke, and every viewer has been in that group.

data.title: PHP team chat
data.reply:
Fix A? No, B.
B breaks stuff.
Discuss again?

world: A case-file headline: the finders' names slam in, 'FOUND BOTH BUGS' is written in marker, and a blue WITH AI stamp lands.
why: The turn is who found the bugs and how. Plain names plus a blue AI stamp set up the finders-versus-fixers question at the end.

world: A paper quote card: the one plain sentence typed to an AI appears word by word, gets highlighted, and a bug doodle crawls out and stays wiggling to the cut.
why: The shock is how short the request was. Reading the exact quote shows how easy it was.

data.role: on what the AI was asked

world: A drawn thermometer climbing toward red, with EXPLOIT ATTEMPT alert cards piling up behind it faster at each step.
why: Leak, then tens of thousands, then millions: the steps climb, so the meter and the card pile-up show the speed without a lonely number.

world: Callback: the opening street. The agencies' order is written in the sky, windows go dark one by one, shutters slam, and the HACKER figure rattles shutters that won't open. Nobody gets in, not even you.
why: The script calls back to 'shutters down', so the same street returns and we now know why it closed and who it shut out.

world: Bare paper in near silence. A zero slams in, 'BREAK-INS' is written under it and circled, and a PLOT TWIST stamp has already landed above.
why: After the meter boils over, silence makes the zero land. The stamp reads as a twist in under a second.

world: A sober typed note: 'UNCONFIRMED ≠ NONE' types out, then 'ATTACKERS' drops and 'STRUGGLING' scrambles in red, credited to Sophos.
why: This is the honest caveat. A plain typed line in a quieter style keeps the twist from overclaiming and credits the source.

world: The street drops back in. The question returns in the sky, shutters slam on 'the shutters', and the HACKER figure walks the doors still knocking.
why: The payoff answers the hook on the same street: so far the closed shutters did the damage, and the hackers are still outside knocking.

world: A quiet split-flap board, like a cricket scoreboard, ticking from 0 up to 34, then 'OVER 34 MILLION' and 'STILL VULNERABLE'.
why: A sober line after the joke: the count ticks up like a running score that isn't over yet.

world: A to-do note written straight to the viewer about their own site, line by line, ending on a red TONIGHT stamp.
why: The viewer's own life: short actions written as a checklist they could follow tonight. No metaphor gets in the way of the instruction.

world: The street one last time. A small robot tagged AI walks the doors checking each lock, FINDERS and FIXERS sprint to the same door, and a red question mark lands and holds.
why: The cliffhanger is a race. Reusing the street closes the visual loop and leaves the question open on one hit.

world: A warm paper street in the viewer's neighbourhood: your clinic, a pharmacy, a hospital tower in the middle and a path lab. Every door is shut and nobody is inside. Big handwritten sky notes follow the voice: the claim, the catch, the question.
why: The hook needs a real world straight away. The AI 'won' at medicine on a street where it never walked into one clinic. The same street carries the loop, so 'what did it win?' is asked over the same shut doors. Every note starts on a phrase that is spoken and ends on the next one, so the sky never runs ahead of the voice.

world: Three index cards on a desk: the system, its 2025 preprint and the journal. Only the journal card gets a PUBLISHED stamp.
why: A quick 'this is real' moment that sets up the two versions of the work: the 2025 preprint and the Science paper. The stamp lands on 'published in Science' and goes only on the Science card, because a preprint is not published. 2025 is shown on its card.

world: The whole case file as a stack of layers (full history, scans, lab results, exam notes, main complaint) that drops in, then lifts apart to show the whole paper. Then only the top slip, the main complaint, slides out and shakes while the rest dim, and a stamp lands on it.
why: One continuous move for two linked beats: 'earlier tests handed over the whole paper' becomes the full file laid open, and 'D.X.O. gets one line' becomes the same file collapsing to a single slip. The kicker is on screen from frame one so the page is never empty. The riser ends on the stamp at 'main complaint'.

world: Your own clinic as a little pipeline: the one-line slip goes to your doctor, who sends questions back and test orders out, and every test sends a yellow bill back.
why: An order slip goes in and decisions come out, made medical. It puts the viewer's own doctor on screen. Holding the same world for the price-tag line makes the 'pretend money' bill an object, not a number.

world: A committee table: four AI name cards are dealt in, and each gets an ON PANEL stamp as its job is named.
why: 'Not one AI' becomes a seated panel with name plates. Each role lands on its own words (suggests diagnoses, picks tests, challenges everyone, watches the bill), so the structure is easy to follow. Sound is thinned so the voice stays on top.

world: A housing society's stack of account books. For once, the committee pulls out the bills and actually stamps them checked.
why: The colony committee, except this one does its job. A drawn ledger being checked lands the joke as a picture, with the stamp on 'the accounts' as the punchline.

world: Two nodes: a red FIRST GUESS slip goes to the ARGUER robot, which bounces it back with 'check again'. 'Anchoring' is named at the end.
why: This shows why the panel argues: the first guess goes in and gets bounced back instead of being accepted. The kicker labels it as the authors' view (they say it 'may' stop the clinging), and the word 'anchoring' gets its own note when it is spoken.

world: A railway-style split-flap board rattles from 0 up to 304, the size of the exam, then names the cases and how they were turned into visits.
why: The number appears as a mechanical count that lands on 304 as it is spoken, and it kicks off the escalation along with the new driving track. The journal is credited in the sub-line, and a second caption turns 'step-by-step visits' into words on the board so the back half of the line has something to see.

world: An exam hall in three nodes: the AI panel's desk, the 304-case paper in the middle, and the generalists' desk. The paper goes to each desk. The AI desk's score is written large on 'eighty-three point two', then the generalists' score on 'thirty-six point one', and both stay up until the scene ends. The source credit (Science paper, Gizmodo) is in the kicker from frame one.
why: Both scores sit in one picture, so 'more than twice' is something you can see. Desks and an exam paper are drawn from the first frame, so the page is never empty. Each score is a labelled note (AI: 83.2%, DOCTORS: 36.1%), so a viewer never has to hold a number by ear. The kicker pays off the preprint/Science cards from scene 1. The riser ends on the AI score.

world: A hype thermometer rushes up while 'AI BEATS DOCTORS!' cartoon headline cards pile up behind it like phone alerts, faster and faster.
why: This is peak escalation: 'more than twice' climbs, then the headline flood makes the hype visible right before the correction. The cards are plainly cartoon headlines, and the 83.2 vs 36.1 stay on the first step so both numbers are still shown.

world: The exam hall returns in three nodes: BOOKS, GENERALISTS and AI PANEL. The books are taken away, the generalists' desk drops to about 22%, and the multiplier changes to nearly 4×. The last clause sends a 'who you compare' envelope across.
why: The previous scene hyped '2×'. This one is the honest correction, built from the same desks so the viewer sees the same people scoring lower, not a new set of numbers. Each figure is a note on its spoken words, and the closing envelope makes 'it depends who you compare' a moving object. Energy stays up because the twist comes next.

world: The music cuts out. Five plain index cards spell out who it really beat and under what conditions, and each gets a red SMALL PRINT stamp.
why: The twist lands in near silence with a scratch, and the stamps cool the hype. Each card matches a phrase in the line, in order (generalists, working alone, rare, tough, not a real clinic), so every stamp lands on its word. 'Small print' is a familiar idiom that needs no setup.

world: The opponent it never faced: a SPECIALISTS slab slides out of a two-slab stack and gets a NOT FACED stamp, with a note giving the narrowing gap as the researchers' own expectation.
why: 'Not specialists' becomes a physical object: the slab that was never tested. The narrowing gap is shown as the researchers' expectation, not ours, with their name written in the note.

world: The pipeline comes back: the AI panel works on a simulated case, and the yellow bill that comes back is marked pretend, with the savings an estimate.
why: This calls back the yellow BILL envelope from the clinic flow, so 'estimated, simulated, not real bills' reads as the same pretend money from earlier.

world: A report-card moment on a sunburst: the opening question scrambles back, then a red RANK #1 stamp lands, qualified by 'in a MOCK TEST' in blue marker.
why: This closes the open loop: the callback question resolves into a topper's stamp, and 'mock test' is circled as the honest qualifier. The burst, the scrambling question and the stamp mean the page is never empty. The riser ends on the RANK #1 stamp.

world: Back on the opening clinic street, quieter now. The doors are still shut. Sky notes follow the voice: no real patient yet, testing still needed, replace doctors? Microsoft: no, meant to augment. The AI robot walks past the shut doors on 'AI chief'.
why: This world callback to scene 0 grounds the payoff: the same unvisited clinics, now with the AI robot on the street. Each note starts on the phrase it illustrates and ends on the next one, so 'MEANT TO AUGMENT' cannot appear before it is spoken. Four buildings and no zoom, so nothing is cropped.

world: A three-node lineup: DOCTOR, HOSPITAL and COMPANY. A WRONG CALL slip is passed along the line, then each suspect wobbles in turn as it is named, and the question is left hanging.
why: The cliffhanger as a lineup with no verdict. The slip travels from company to hospital to doctor, each suspect wobbles on its own spoken word, and nothing is stamped, so the question stays open. Every note and cue is taken from the closing line.

world: A paper strip of roadside freight depots: AI depot, warehouse, data center, truck yard. They draw on, then every door gets the same padlock. Handwritten notes in the sky follow the voice.
why: The hook says $100M+ of AI freight was stolen and that the pattern is paperwork. Intact locks on every door show nothing was broken into. The same street returns for the payoff.

world: A railway-style split-flap board on paper, rolling up to the price of one AI server rack, then calling it a vault on wheels.
why: The digits roll up to about $3,000,000 on 'Overhaul says', with the source credited on the board. The caption lands on the number, then on the vault line, in spoken order.

world: A truck tracker sends its real dot to a dispatcher's dashboard. Then a fake signal sneaks in through a back door and the dot lies.
why: It explains GPS spoofing as a lying dot, a real dot first and then a fake one. It claims only what the script says: one big theft.

world: A thermometer of force against deception climbs step by step while a few DECEPTION alert cards pile up behind it.
why: 'Don't blame the satellites yet' turns the story. A climbing meter, with Overhaul credited in the kicker, builds to the 92% stat.

world: A cartoon matchmaking office. A broker aunty introduces a shipper uncle to a trucker.
why: The joke explains a freight broker in a second. The broker points and moves on every phrase, so the picture never sits still.

world: Index cards of fake loads fly in under a hacked-broker heading, and each gets a red BAIT stamp.
why: Step one is shown as an action. The hacked account posts fake loads and the cards are stamped BAIT, which is the only purpose the script gives them.

world: Thieves send a link to a trucking firm's phone. One click opens the back door and the firm's account bids on a real load.
why: A slipped-in note that makes someone obey a stranger is what a malicious link does. The red takeover and the bid keep step two in one picture.

world: The viewer's own family chat on a hand-drawn phone. 'Mummy' messages the dhobi, but it isn't mummy. Tagged as a re-enactment.
why: The kicker says it is the same trick at home. It explains the hijacked account in the viewer's own life: a trusted name in a chat is enough to hand over the goods.

data.title: Mummy (hijacked) → Dhobi
data.prompt: Give dad's suits to my friend.

world: Two cartoon drivers side by side at the truck stop. One is cheerful and unaware. The other turns shifty.
why: The beat names two kinds of collector. Two people, each with an arrow, make the either/or readable at once, and only the accomplice turns suspicious.

world: Bare paper in near silence. Two index cards, LOAD 1 and LOAD 2, get a red HIT stamp.
why: This is the twist: the con turns physical. The music cuts and a scratch lands. The stamps act out the ramming on screen.

world: A quote card with a doodled padlock. Scott Cornell of SPG is credited and 'weren't properly vetted' is swiped with the highlighter.
why: It bridges force and trust. Even the rammed loads are tied to verification failures, not to the trucks. A real quote is credited to a named person.

world: Callback: the opening strip of depots, every padlock still shut. The camera pans down to the slab they all stand on, TRUST, and it cracks. Sky notes list Cornell's fixes.
why: The payoff in one move: the locks held and the shared foundation of trust failed. The notes give Cornell's two fixes and why paper bills are the weak point.

world: Words on bare paper. A scrambled 'borrowed login' resolves into the question for the viewer, and the last line is circled so the question stays on screen.
why: The cliffhanger re-points at the video's real trick: an account that looks right. It turns the question onto the viewer's own screen and holds it.
